claims.text: The initial nanoparticles contain Pt, Pd, Rh, Ru, and Ir in equiatomic proportions.
The initial nanoparticles are crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution.
Structural and chemical stability is governed by the interplay of oxidation-driven selective surface segregation and thermal diffusion kinetics.
Under oxidizing conditions, differential oxidation kinetics drive elemental segregation at the nanoparticle surface.
Slower heating provides sufficient time for oxidation-coupled diffusion and therefore increases surface segregation.
Rapid heating kinetically suppresses diffusion processes that lead to segregation.
An inert atmosphere suppresses segregation and helps maintain the homogeneous solid solution.
Thermal treatment can produce surface oxide layers and atomic diffusion along grain boundaries and within nanoparticle cores.
Differences in oxidation kinetics and intrinsic metal surface energies promote selective oxidation and surface segregation.
Slow heating allows diffusion to progress toward thermodynamic equilibrium.
Diffusion toward equilibrium can generate compositional gradients or core-shell structures.
Slow heating in an oxidizing environment will produce measurable oxide layers and surface compositional gradients relative to the initial state.
Rapidly heated or inert-atmosphere samples will exhibit little or no segregation and will retain a uniform solid-solution structure.
The initial baseline has no significant surface oxide formation or compositional gradients.
The predicted relationships apply over 473–1923 K when oxygen partial pressure, ramp rate, and dwell time are controlled.
Conditions outside the specified range or uncontrolled atmospheres may introduce additional phase transformations or oxidation phenomena.
